summary:
Santa Fe province has no trans-specific statute of its own in the source inventory. What a trans visitor in Santa Fe faces is Argentina's national framework, which extends to every province: Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the national identity document (DNI) has carried an 'X' marker option since 2021.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive decree rather than by repeal. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei published DNU 62/2025, amending Article 11 of the 2012 Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions, alongside DNU 61/2025, which alters prison-sentencing law in order to change the placement of transgender detainees. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province, including Santa Fe. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations interviewed by Agencia Presentes called both measures unconstitutional and said that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth; the decrees face judicial challenge, and the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Trans activists in Argentina told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that the community faces a 'chaotic, desperate' situation under President Milei, who eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1 per cent of public-sector posts and which activists say is no longer being implemented. Activists reported that the 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator is therefore not applied in that case as it now stands.

Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's 2012 regime was described by the United Nations as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and the country's marriage-equality law of 2010 predates comparable legislation across much of Latin America. The narrowing of that framework since early 2025 therefore runs against the direction of the statute on the books, which is why rights monitors record deterioration rather than reform.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio's 2025 total of at least 227 hate crimes was reported by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026 as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed by the Washington Blade on 4 April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

Outright International's negative assessment of organisation registration suggests a constraint on the civil-society infrastructure that visitors and residents alike would rely on for local guidance, legal referral and emergency support.
localsOnly:
Residents of Santa Fe live under the national Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1 per cent of public-sector posts for trans workers. Activists told the Washington Blade that the quota is no longer being implemented following the elimination of the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, and that trans hires made under it have been dismissed.

DNU 61/2025 alters the prison-sentencing framework and governs the placement of transgender detainees. It applies to every province, so the treatment of a trans person remanded or sentenced in Santa Fe's prisons stands under that national decree rather than under any provincial rule documented here.

The ban on gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions for under-18s, introduced by DNU 62/2025 on 5 February 2025, reaches trans minors resident in Santa Fe, and legal experts and LGBT+ organisations say the abrupt suspension of ongoing adolescent treatment endangers trans youth.

Legal gender recognition under Law 26.743, including the 'X' marker available on the DNI since 2021, remains the process available to Santa Fe residents for changing registered sex and name.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the judicial challenge to DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 is unresolved in the sources available here; legal experts and LGBT+ organisations petitioned the courts to intervene, but no ruling is recorded.

Whether Santa Fe province has adopted its own provincial anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute with specific reference to gender identity is not sourced in this inventory. National and provincial protections are asserted generally in the parent framework without a Santa Fe instrument being named.

No Santa Fe-specific figures for hate crimes, police conduct toward trans people, or the practical application of the prison-placement decree appear in the inventory; the 227 recorded hate crimes for 2025 are national totals without a provincial breakdown.

Whether the Trans Labor Quota Law continues to operate in Santa Fe's provincial public administration after the elimination of the national ministry is not documented; the non-implementation reported by activists was described at national level.
